Prose:
The guard’s hand hovered over the staff, the weapon trembling slightly in his grip. Caelen saw the calculation behind the hesitation. The masked man at the table had not looked up from his ledger, but Caelen knew that gaze was all-encompassing. If he acted on impulse, he would break the flow of control.

"Bad systems need bad inputs," Caelen said again, forcing a laugh that cracked halfway through, sounding more like a broken hinge than amusement. "She’s just a variable you haven’t calibrated yet."

He stepped back further, creating a deliberate buffer zone between himself, the guard’s staff, and her trembling form. He kept his eyes locked on the guard’s masked face, watching for any sign of renewed aggression or impatience.

The guard scoffed, raising the butt of his staff again, but the motion lacked its previous certainty. Caelen leaned into his own clumsiness, letting the heaviness of his new frame drag his shoulders down to make him appear even more unstable. "If you swing now," Caelen continued, his voice low and steady despite the alien harshness of the words rolling off his tongue, "you break your rhythm. You waste your strength on something that doesn’t move. Look at me."

He gestured vaguely with a bound hand toward the man in purple sitting at the rickety table.

The masked man had ceased flipping his ledger and was now watching the exchange with pale, unreadable eyes. The scarred captive sat slumped against an overturned crate nearby, looking less like a prisoner of consequence and more like discarded furniture. "That one," Caelen said, nodding toward the overseer. "He watches everything. If you make a scene here, he sees it. He decides who lives and who dies based on how well you perform your duties. You don’t want to miss his approval."

The guard hesitated. The logic was sound, even if the premise was terrifying. Attacking him would be inefficient; surviving the overseer’s displeasure was a higher priority than any single victim. Slowly, the guard lowered his staff completely, stepping back to resume his patrol route without another word.

Caelen exhaled sharply, the tension leaving his chest only to be replaced by a dull, throbbing ache in his ribs. He glanced toward the masked man in purple, who had resumed tapping his black-tipped cane against the stone floor with a rhythmic indifference. The scarred captive remained slumped, his authority shattered, and the young woman was still kneeling, shaking violently.

The brief respite had been purchased, but it wasn’t freedom. It was merely a pause in the countdown to the next beat. He could feel the phantom sensation of bruising bone beneath his skin where the staff had struck him earlier. He resolved to keep talking, to keep playing the fool while he gathered intelligence. If the masked man was the true master here, then Caelen needed to understand the rules of the game before he could try to change them. He would be the idiot they wanted him to be, and in that role, perhaps he might find a way to survive long enough to stop being one.

He shifted his weight cautiously, testing the limits of his restraints without drawing attention. The silence allowed him to assess the pen’s layout: the position of the other captives huddled in the gloom, the patrol route the guard had just taken, and the distance to the cell door where two figures stood with spears resting against their shoulders. He accepted his constrained agency as the only currency available right now. Pain and confusion were not obstacles; they were the conditions of his existence here.
